writeup.1: In 1981 a club pro named Rick Reimers quit his job in Northern California and got in the car to drive north to Montana, to ski and think. The car radio was broken, so he spent the whole drive designing a golf bag in his head. What came out the other end was a nylon carry bag that weighed less than half what the leather and vinyl bags of the day weighed.
writeup.2: That was the BACK 9, and it was more interesting than it was successful. The FRONT 9 arrived in 1984 with a moulded top and bottom, sold properly, and became the shape every other carry bag copied. It also earned Sun Mountain the job of building the L8 bag for Ping, which put a Missoula startup in the position of manufacturing for one of golf’s giants.
writeup.3: Then, in 1986, they put legs on it. The Eclipse is the bag Sun Mountain is credited with inventing, and its patented stand mechanism is now hinged onto almost every carry bag in the game. They ran the same trick twice more. The Speed Cart in 1999 folded down small enough that people bought one, and a walking-cart category appeared where there had not been one. The ClubGlider in 2008 put retractable legs on a travel bag, so an airport stopped being a workout.
writeup.4: Here is the part that gets left out. Reimers ran the company for 41 years as founder, director and sole shareholder, with no partners, no investors and no board. In March 2022 he sold Sun Mountain Sports to Solace Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, and kept the scooter business. The bags are still assembled in Missoula, which remains unusual for the category. The fabrics come from Asia, and the company says “assembled in the USA” rather than made, which is the honest version.
writeup.5: The line runs across four categories: bags from the $224 Eclipse up to a $1,200 leather stand bag, push carts, travel covers, and small goods down to a $35 headcover. Three of those four are categories Sun Mountain either created or reshaped, which is a strange thing to say about the sensible default.
